Series::lcm¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::lcm(const Series& other) const
Series& Series::lcm_(const Series& other)
Series& Series::lcm_(const Series& rhs) const

What It Does¶

lcm() finds the first non-negative multiple shared by each aligned pair of integers. If a describes a task that repeats every four ticks and b one that repeats every six ticks, lcm(a, b) is twelve: the first tick at which those two cycles meet again.

The operation is elementwise and broadcastable. It does not reduce a whole series to one scheduling period. That distinction lets a row of reference periods be compared with every row in a table of observed periods in one call.

For nonzero pairs, GCD and LCM divide the same information in opposite ways:

gcd(a, b) * lcm(a, b) = |a * b|

Conceptually, lcm(a, b) is |a / gcd(a, b) * b|; the divide-first form explains which common factors are removed before the remaining factors are combined. If either input is zero, the result is defined as zero.

Conventions, matching std::lcm:

  • the result is always >= 0, regardless of the signs of the inputs

  • lcm(x, 0) == 0 for any x

Integer-only: a floating-point or complex input raises.

Parameters¶

other (const Series&): the second integer operand, broadcast against the receiver. The result uses the promoted integer dtype of both operands.

Returns¶

Series or Series& A new series containing the non-negative pairwise multiples, with the broadcast shape and promoted integer dtype. lcm_() writes the result into the receiver while preserving its storage, shape, and dtype.

Raises if either operand is a floating-point or complex series.

Gradient¶

lcm() is a discrete integer operation and is not differentiable.

In-Place Form¶

lcm_() is the in-place sibling of lcm(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — lcm_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series(std::vector<std::int64_t>{4, 6}, {2});
auto y = pluss::make_series(std::vector<std::int64_t>{6, 9}, {2});

x.lcm_(y);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[12, 18]

Examples¶

Example 1. lcm(x, 0) is 0; signs are dropped.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({4, 6, 0}).lcm(pluss::make_series({6, 8, 5})));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[12, 24, 0]

lcm(4, 6) = 12, lcm(6, 8) = 24, lcm(0, 5) = 0.

Example 2. One row of cycle lengths can be broadcast across many schedules.

auto observed = pluss::make_series({{-12, 18, 0}, {20, -27, 14}});
auto reference = pluss::make_series({{8, 6, 5}});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, observed.lcm(reference));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 24 18  0 ⎤
⎣ 40 54 70 ⎦

Read the first column as two independent synchronization questions. Periods 12 and 8 next coincide at 24; periods 20 and 8 next coincide at 40. In the third column, the zero period makes the first answer zero by convention, while 14 and 5 are coprime and therefore require the full product, 70.

Example 3. Use gcd() and lcm() together when both the shared unit and the shared cycle matter.

auto a = pluss::make_series({12, 18, 14});
auto b = pluss::make_series({8, 6, 5});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.gcd(b)) << '\n';
pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.lcm(b));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 6, 1]
Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[24, 18, 70]

The GCD gives the largest exact unit common to each pair. The LCM gives the smallest complete span containing both periods. These are complementary questions, so neither method substitutes for the other.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Integer inputs only; a float operand raises.

  • lcm(x, 0) is 0, which is a valid multiple of everything.

  • The result is never negative.

  • Large valid answers can exceed the promoted integer dtype. Widen narrow operands with to(ScalarType::Int64) before the call, and remember that even int64 has a finite range.

  • Broadcasting may produce a shape larger than the receiver. That works for lcm(), but not for lcm_(), which must preserve receiver storage and shape.

  • Not differentiable.

Summary¶

lcm(a, b) is the elementwise least common multiple:

  • |a * b| / gcd(a, b); lcm(x, 0) = 0; result >= 0

  • integer inputs only

  • not differentiable

  • lcm_() is the in-place form

See Also¶

  • Series::gcd: the greatest common divisor this is built from.

  • Series::factor: the prime factorization behind both.
